title: My ordinary day
goal: Describe your daily routine in order and use reflexive verbs such as se lever and se coucher.
bekal: tell the story of a day with sequencing words
use reflexive verbs: *je me lève*, *tu te couches*
use *aller* and *faire*, which turn up everywhere
wave: Go back to **Unit 6** first: take ten verbs from its table, say all six forms out loud, then make the *je* form negative.

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Une journée ordinaire
dialogs.intro: Thomas is curious how Budi organizes his day.

lines.speaker: Thomas:
lines.text: Tu te lèves à quelle heure d'habitude ?
lines.id: What time do you usually get up?
lines.literal: you yourself raise at which hour of-habit?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Je me lève à six heures et demie.
lines.id: I get up at half past six.
lines.literal: I myself raise at six hours and half.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Je me douche, je m'habille et je prends mon petit-déjeuner.
lines.id: I shower, get dressed and have breakfast.
lines.literal: I myself shower, I myself dress and I take my little-lunch.

lines.speaker: Thomas:
lines.id: What do you eat in the morning?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Du pain et du café. Ensuite je vais à l'université.
lines.id: Bread and coffee. Then I go to the university.
lines.literal: some bread and some coffee. next I go to the-university.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: En bus. Le trajet dure vingt minutes.
lines.id: By bus. The trip takes twenty minutes.
lines.literal: in bus. the trip lasts twenty minutes.

lines.speaker: Thomas:
lines.text: Et le soir, qu'est-ce que tu fais ?
lines.id: And in the evening, what do you do?
lines.literal: and the evening, what is-it-that you do?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Je travaille, puis je rentre et je dîne vers vingt-trois heures.
lines.id: I work, then I go home and have dinner around 11 p.m.
lines.literal: I work, then I return and I dine toward twenty-three hours.

lines.speaker: Thomas:
lines.id: So you go to bed late!

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Oui. Le week-end, je ne fais rien. C'est sacré.
lines.id: Yes. On weekends I do nothing. It's sacred.
lines.literal: yes. the weekend, I not do nothing. it-is sacred.

notes: **Reflexive verbs come with a twin pronoun.** *Je me lève* is literally "I raise myself". English just says "I get up", so the *me* feels redundant — but without it, *je lève* means "I lift (something)".

**The pronoun follows the subject:** *je **me**, tu **te**, il **se**, nous **nous**, vous **vous**, ils **se***. Before a vowel, *me/te/se* are cut short: *je m'habille*, *tu t'appelles*, *il s'appelle*.

**Le petit-déjeuner** is literally "the little lunch" — because *déjeuner* on its own means lunch. The order: *petit-déjeuner* (morning), *déjeuner* (midday), *dîner* (evening). All three can also be verbs: *je déjeune à midi*.
**Tu y vas** — the little word *y* replaces a place already mentioned, like "there" in English. It's said ee and goes in front of the verb. You don't need to master it at A1; just recognize it.
**En bus, à pied.** Transport you get inside takes **en** (*en bus, en voiture, en train, en avion*); transport you sit on top of takes **à** (*à pied, à vélo, à cheval*).
**Le week-end** is borrowed straight from English and is officially in French dictionaries. With the article *le* it means "every weekend" — just as *le matin* means "every morning".
**Je ne fais rien** — notice that *rien* replaces *pas* rather than adding to it. A pattern you already set up in Unit 6.

grammars.title: Reflexive verbs
body: Called *verbes pronominaux*. A group of verbs whose action turns back on the subject — and most daily-routine activities belong to it.
after: The negative wraps around **the pronoun and the verb together**: *je **ne** me lève **pas** tôt*. The pronoun goes inside the *ne … pas* hug.

The most common ones: *se réveiller* (to wake up), *se lever* (to get up), *se doucher* (to shower), *se laver* (to wash), *se brosser les dents* (to brush your teeth), *se préparer* (to get ready), *se reposer* (to rest), *se dépêcher* (to hurry), *s'amuser* (to have fun), *se coucher* (to go to bed), *s'endormir* (to fall asleep).
⚠️ *Se lever* changes e to è in four forms: *je lève, tu lèves, il lève, ils lèvent* — but *nous levons, vous levez*. The accent isn't decoration; without it the e would be silent.

grammars.title: Aller and faire
body: Two verbs that turn up in almost every conversation, and both are very irregular. There's no way around learning them by heart.
after: ⚠️ *Nous faisons* is said noo fuh-ZOHN, not noo feh-ZOHN. The only word in French where *ai* sounds like the light *uh*.
*Vous faites* and *vous êtes* are two of the three verbs whose *vous* form doesn't end in -ez. The third is *vous dites* (you say).

*Faire* covers many activities that English expresses with different verbs: *faire les courses* (to go shopping), *faire la cuisine* (to cook), *faire le ménage* (to clean the house), *faire du sport* (to play sports), *faire attention* (to be careful).

grammars.title: Putting things in order
body: Linking words that turn a list of activities into a story.

sections.title: A day from morning to night

blocks.title: Where to? — au, à la, à l'
items: *à* merges with *le* to make **au**, and with *les* to make **aux**. With *la* and *l'* it doesn't change.
*Je vais **à la** bibliothèque, **à la** maison, **à la** gare.* (feminine)
⚠️ Writing *à le cinéma* is a flat-out grammar mistake — this merging is compulsory, not optional.

items: I get up at half past six.
Then I go to the university.
On weekends, I don't do anything.
